Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key findings and impressions:  
  - Adult patient with acute-onset wheeze and progressive dyspnea beginning ~2 days after dust exposure. History of childhood asthma and seasonal hay fever supports an atopic/reactive airways cause. No chest pain, dizziness, syncope, or systemic allergic features documented. No objective respiratory measurements or examination findings recorded in the encounter.

- Working diagnosis and management priorities:  
  - Working diagnosis: Likely asthma exacerbation / allergic/irritant-triggered bronchospasm (dust-triggered). Management priority is to assess severity with objective measures (oxygen saturation, respiratory exam, PEFR/spirometry) and treat bronchospasm and airway inflammation as indicated.

- Relevant differential diagnoses from DDx (consistent with transcript):  
  1) Asthma exacerbation (allergic/irritant-triggered bronchospasm) — High likelihood. Reason: temporal relation to dust exposure, history of childhood asthma and atopy, progressive wheeze and speech limitation.  
  2) Allergic upper airway reaction with secondary bronchospasm — Moderate likelihood. Reason: atopy and clear inhaled trigger; lacks systemic anaphylactic features.  
  3) Acute viral bronchitis / reactive airways post-infection — Moderate likelihood. Reason: can produce wheeze and progressive dyspnea; less supported here due to immediate dust exposure and absence of infection symptoms.

- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:  No conflicts noted — DDx aligns with transcript history and clinician reasoning.

Management Plan

- Immediate / short-term actions documented in transcript:  
  - Patient advised to attend a clinic/GP for in-person assessment.  
  - Clinic assessment to include pulse oximetry (finger oximeter) and further respiratory examination/testing (PEFR/spirometry) to determine severity.  
  - If available, the clinician advised taking an oral antihistamine for presumed allergic trigger prior to the clinic visit; patient does not have one at home and was advised she can obtain one OTC (~£4–6) or get a prescription from GP.  
  - Clinician noted patient may require oral corticosteroids depending on assessment results but will not prescribe until after in-person testing.  
  - A letter will be sent to the patient's GP via the app to inform them; in-person GP consultation estimated ~10 minutes.

- Follow-up and monitoring:  
  - Attend GP/clinic for the planned assessment and objective respiratory tests.  
  - Management (bronchodilator therapy, oral corticosteroids, further investigations) to be decided after in-person assessment results.

- Patient education documented:  
  - Advised regarding antihistamine as an initial measure if suspecting allergy. (Cost estimate and availability discussed.)

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- 1) Asthma exacerbation (allergic/irritant-triggered bronchospasm) — High likelihood.  
  - Justification: Acute wheeze after dust exposure, history of childhood asthma and hay fever, progressive nocturnal worsening and speech limitation suggesting significant airflow obstruction.

- 2) Allergic bronchospasm / localized respiratory allergic reaction — Moderate likelihood.  
  - Justification: Temporal link to inhaled dust exposure and atopy; absence of systemic anaphylactic features favors localized bronchospasm.

- 3) Acute viral bronchitis / reactive airways post-infection — Moderate likelihood.  
  - Justification: Can present with wheeze and progressive dyspnea in atopic/reactive patients; less supported here due to immediate dust trigger and lack of infectious symptoms.
